title: Timothy Ali / Product designer
text:
i’m tim.
Timothy Ali

Product designer. I design interfaces and design systems, and build the front end. Based in Denver and open to remote work, full-time or contract.

SELECTED WORK
RESUME
->
Selected work
TOOLBOX

A desktop app I designed and built for getting brand files ready to hand off. It packages logos, exports palettes, makes type sheets, and converts images.

PARC

A new identity and website for the NFT club I cofounded in 2021, including a custom pixel typeface, live collection stats, and a rowing game.

JADE AESTHETICS

Two websites for a medical spa. I launched the first in Framer, then rebuilt it in Next.js with a page for each treatment.

title: PARC: NFT club identity and website / Timothy Ali

controls.text: Play video: PARC After Darc starting-soon screen: a pixel sun over the sea with a rowboat drifting p

text:
PARC
PARC

I cofounded Pixel Ape Rowboat Club in 2021 and have led its branding and art direction since. In 2026, I redesigned the identity around the apes’ 5×5 grid and made a typeface for it, PARC Pixel. Then I built a new website with live stats, a gallery, merch, and a rowing game.

ROLE
Cofounder · brand, art direction & website
TEAM
Cofounders xrpl_adam, sloppy, and stove
TIMELINE
Ongoing · site live since September 2026
TOOLS
Illustrator, Python (fontTools), SvelteKit, Svelte 5, TypeScript, Canvas, Vercel, Neon, Claude Code
LIVE
parcxrpl.com
->
01 / 11
WHERE IT STARTED

PARC started in November 2021 as a joke. People were treating pixel apes as status symbols, and we thought that was ridiculous. Bored Apes had yachts. Ours had rowboats. 10,000 pixel apes on the XRP Ledger, no clout included.

People stayed anyway. By 2026, PARC had four collections, a Twitch show, an arcade, merch, and its own lore. I run it with xrpl_adam on development, sloppy on marketing, and stove drawing the apes with me. The old identity no longer matched what we were making.

The apes were drawn with the Game Boy Advance Pokémon games in mind: flat color, chunky pixels, sprites you could recognize at a glance. We built them a world of islands, rowboats, volcanoes, and wooden huts, and the rebrand had to look like it belonged there.

02 / 11
AN EARLIER DIRECTION

Around 2024, I tried splitting the club into three branches: The Rowboat Club with an oar, The Parcade with a red joystick, and The Nightclub with a red microphone, each with a black pixel wordmark. We liked how it looked, but it felt too serious and dark for PARC, so we set it aside.

Set aside, around 2024

03 / 11
REDRAWING THE LOGO

The old logo was a cartoon ape with thick outlines and a bubbly wordmark. It didn’t look much like the pixel art around it. I drew the new logo on the apes’ 5×5 grid and put it on a white sign with notched corners.

The team was attached to the old identity and worried about how the community would react. This time I showed them the finished logo on its sign and asked them to trust me. The comments after launch were encouraging.

Before, 2021 / after, 2026

THE REACTION
01
“I know I like the new banner and logo” / RedHotDankMoist, Discord
02
“Love it, great website update, looks amazing” / @BrandoWoodz, X
04 / 11
LOGO, COLOR, AND SPACING

I made a wide logo, a square lockup, and an oar badge, all on the same cell grid with notched corners and two cells of clear space around them. The final artwork is merged paths, so it goes straight into print and web files.

The palette has five colors. The logo uses four of them, and everything else uses one at a time. I gave hex values for web and CMYK for print, and ruled out yellow type on white because it’s hard to read.

The oar works as a favicon, a badge, and a divider. I also put it on the typeface’s equals key so it’s easy to use in a line of text.

05 / 11
THE TYPEFACE

I built PARC Pixel from the four letters in the logo, keeping their one-cell strokes, open counters, and stepped diagonals. Scripts generate the family from the logo’s grid: three weights and a monospaced version for scores and prices, with 56 glyphs in each. It took four days from the first glyph to the finished family.

The scripts struggled with some characters, especially the number 2. I built a small editor to place pixels by hand, then used the scripts to compile the fonts. I drew 29 glyphs across the family this way, including the bold 2, the oar, and all three at-signs, and checked them in words at reading size.

06 / 11
STREAMS, MERCH, AND SOCIAL

Outside the site, the identity shows up on Discord, X, Twitch, merch, and the arcade. After Darc, the club’s Twitch show, has its own graphics and a starting-soon animation.

07 / 11
THE WEBSITE

PARC had outgrown its Squarespace site. The club now had four collections, a token, a Twitch show, an arcade, and merch. I designed a new site to bring them together and built it with Claude Code, directing the work and reviewing every screen.

I built the site around the logo’s pixel grid and the club’s island setting. The Clubhouse, Gallery, and PARCade each have their own place in that world. The home page opens with the wordmark on a notched paper card. Inner pages use a jungle canopy, drifting clouds, and a wooden sign for the title and introduction.

The notch shows up everywhere: 6px on buttons, 10px on cards, 12px on panels. Buttons sit on a darker base, lift on hover, and drop when you press them. The motion is pixel-based too. Buttons move in steps, water shifts one cell at a time, and dropdowns open line by line. With reduced motion on, the animated backgrounds hold still.

08 / 11
STATS FIRST

I put Stats first in the navigation so holders could find it fast. It has floor prices, trading volume, holders, and listings for each collection, plus $OAR token data. The numbers come from the ledger and marketplace APIs, and daily snapshots feed the charts, going back to launch.

09 / 11
GALLERY & CLUBHOUSE

In the Gallery, apes hang on clotheslines between two trees. Selecting a frame opens a plaque with the ape’s name. My first version turned wheel input into sideways scrolling. It was awkward to use, so I switched to normal vertical scrolling.

The Clubhouse took three layouts to get right. It ended up with a TV playing the Twitch stream, a trophy shelf, and a corkboard for events, suspended from branches. I checked the ropes at different screen widths to keep them attached.

10 / 11
PARCADE

PARCade is an arcade cabinet with a green CRT, scanlines, a joystick, and buttons that work the menu. On the homepage, a smaller screen shows the game cover next to live high scores, with scenery built from the game’s sprites around it.

I also made Rowboat Racer, where an ape rows down a five-lane river dodging logs, reefs, and ziggurats. I drew the sprites on a 3px grid. The riverbanks change between beach, jungle, rock, and village scenery on each run. The server replays a run before accepting its score on the leaderboard.

11 / 11
MERCH & COMMUNITY

I originally planned to link out to the merch store. Using its API meant I could put the catalog on the site and send people to the store only for checkout. Each section got a small detail of its own. After Darc has TV static, chat bubbles drift past the Discord section, and the LARC teaser has a working terminal. The 404 sign says you rowed off the map.

On a phone

OUTCOME
01
A logo library in print and web formats: the wide logo, the square lockup, and the oar
02
PARC Pixel: three weights plus a mono, 56 glyphs each, the only typeface on the site
03
parcxrpl.com: seven pages plus the error pages, live since September 2026
04
Live data from the ledger, xrp.cafe, the AMM, the Fourthwall storefront, and the game leaderboard
NEXT / [03]
JADE AESTHETICS ->
[02] / 007
TELL ME WHAT YOU’RE BUILDING ->

PARC started in November 2021 as a joke. People were treating pixel apes as status symbols, and we thought that was ridiculous. Bored Apes had yachts. Ours had rowboats. 10,000 pixel apes on the XRP Ledger, no clout included.

People stayed anyway. By 2026, PARC had four collections, a Twitch show, an arcade, merch, and its own lore. I run it with xrpl_adam on development, sloppy on marketing, and stove drawing the apes with me. The old identity no longer matched what we were making.

The apes were drawn with the Game Boy Advance Pokémon games in mind: flat color, chunky pixels, sprites you could recognize at a glance. We built them a world of islands, rowboats, volcanoes, and wooden huts, and the rebrand had to look like it belonged there.

02 / 11
AN EARLIER DIRECTION

Around 2024, I tried splitting the club into three branches: The Rowboat Club with an oar, The Parcade with a red joystick, and The Nightclub with a red microphone, each with a black pixel wordmark. We liked how it looked, but it felt too serious and dark for PARC, so we set it aside.

SET ASIDE, AROUND 2024

03 / 11
REDRAWING THE LOGO

The old logo was a cartoon ape with thick outlines and a bubbly wordmark. It didn’t look much like the pixel art around it. I drew the new logo on the apes’ 5×5 grid and put it on a white sign with notched corners.

The team was attached to the old identity and worried about how the community would react. This time I showed them the finished logo on its sign and asked them to trust me. The comments after launch were encouraging.

BEFORE, 2021 / AFTER, 2026

THE REACTION
01
“I know I like the new banner and logo” / RedHotDankMoist, Discord
02
“Love it, great website update, looks amazing” / @BrandoWoodz, X
04 / 11
LOGO, COLOR, AND SPACING

I made a wide logo, a square lockup, and an oar badge, all on the same cell grid with notched corners and two cells of clear space around them. The final artwork is merged paths, so it goes straight into print and web files.

The palette has five colors. The logo uses four of them, and everything else uses one at a time. I gave hex values for web and CMYK for print, and ruled out yellow type on white because it’s hard to read.

The oar works as a favicon, a badge, and a divider. I also put it on the typeface’s equals key so it’s easy to use in a line of text.

05 / 11
THE TYPEFACE

I built PARC Pixel from the four letters in the logo, keeping their one-cell strokes, open counters, and stepped diagonals. Scripts generate the family from the logo’s grid: three weights and a monospaced version for scores and prices, with 56 glyphs in each. It took four days from the first glyph to the finished family.

The scripts struggled with some characters, especially the number 2. I built a small editor to place pixels by hand, then used the scripts to compile the fonts. I drew 29 glyphs across the family this way, including the bold 2, the oar, and all three at-signs, and checked them in words at reading size.

06 / 11
STREAMS, MERCH, AND SOCIAL

Outside the site, the identity shows up on Discord, X, Twitch, merch, and the arcade. After Darc, the club’s Twitch show, has its own graphics and a starting-soon animation.

07 / 11
THE WEBSITE

PARC had outgrown its Squarespace site. The club now had four collections, a token, a Twitch show, an arcade, and merch. I designed a new site to bring them together and built it with Claude Code, directing the work and reviewing every screen.

I built the site around the logo’s pixel grid and the club’s island setting. The Clubhouse, Gallery, and PARCade each have their own place in that world. The home page opens with the wordmark on a notched paper card. Inner pages use a jungle canopy, drifting clouds, and a wooden sign for the title and introduction.

The notch shows up everywhere: 6px on buttons, 10px on cards, 12px on panels. Buttons sit on a darker base, lift on hover, and drop when you press them. The motion is pixel-based too. Buttons move in steps, water shifts one cell at a time, and dropdowns open line by line. With reduced motion on, the animated backgrounds hold still.

08 / 11
STATS FIRST

I put Stats first in the navigation so holders could find it fast. It has floor prices, trading volume, holders, and listings for each collection, plus $OAR token data. The numbers come from the ledger and marketplace APIs, and daily snapshots feed the charts, going back to launch.

09 / 11
GALLERY & CLUBHOUSE

In the Gallery, apes hang on clotheslines between two trees. Selecting a frame opens a plaque with the ape’s name. My first version turned wheel input into sideways scrolling. It was awkward to use, so I switched to normal vertical scrolling.

The Clubhouse took three layouts to get right. It ended up with a TV playing the Twitch stream, a trophy shelf, and a corkboard for events, suspended from branches. I checked the ropes at different screen widths to keep them attached.

10 / 11
PARCADE

PARCade is an arcade cabinet with a green CRT, scanlines, a joystick, and buttons that work the menu. On the homepage, a smaller screen shows the game cover next to live high scores, with scenery built from the game’s sprites around it.

I also made Rowboat Racer, where an ape rows down a five-lane river dodging logs, reefs, and ziggurats. I drew the sprites on a 3px grid. The riverbanks change between beach, jungle, rock, and village scenery on each run. The server replays a run before accepting its score on the leaderboard.

11 / 11
MERCH & COMMUNITY

I originally planned to link out to the merch store. Using its API meant I could put the catalog on the site and send people to the store only for checkout. Each section got a small detail of its own. After Darc has TV static, chat bubbles drift past the Discord section, and the LARC teaser has a working terminal. The 404 sign says you rowed off the map.

ON A PHONE

OUTCOME
01
A logo library in print and web formats: the wide logo, the square lockup, and the oar
02
PARC Pixel: three weights plus a mono, 56 glyphs each, the only typeface on the site
03
parcxrpl.com: seven pages plus the error pages, live since September 2026
04
Live data from the ledger, xrp.cafe, the AMM, the Fourthwall storefront, and the game leaderboard
NEXT / [03]

The old logo was a cartoon ape with thick outlines and a bubbly wordmark. It didn’t look much like the pixel art around it. I drew the new logo on the apes’ 5×5 grid and put it on a white sign with notched corners.

The team was attached to the old identity and worried about how the community would react. This time I showed them the finished logo on its sign and asked them to trust me. The comments after launch were encouraging.

Before, 2021 / after, 2026

THE REACTION
01
“I know I like the new banner and logo” / RedHotDankMoist, Discord
02
“Love it, great website update, looks amazing” / @BrandoWoodz, X
04 / 11
LOGO, COLOR, AND SPACING

I made a wide logo, a square lockup, and an oar badge, all on the same cell grid with notched corners and two cells of clear space around them. The final artwork is merged paths, so it goes straight into print and web files.

The palette has five colors. The logo uses four of them, and everything else uses one at a time. I gave hex values for web and CMYK for print, and ruled out yellow type on white because it’s hard to read.

The oar works as a favicon, a badge, and a divider. I also put it on the typeface’s equals key so it’s easy to use in a line of text.

05 / 11
THE TYPEFACE

I built PARC Pixel from the four letters in the logo, keeping their one-cell strokes, open counters, and stepped diagonals. Scripts generate the family from the logo’s grid: three weights and a monospaced version for scores and prices, with 56 glyphs in each. It took four days from the first glyph to the finished family.

The scripts struggled with some characters, especially the number 2. I built a small editor to place pixels by hand, then used the scripts to compile the fonts. I drew 29 glyphs across the family this way, including the bold 2, the oar, and all three at-signs, and checked them in words at reading size.

06 / 11
STREAMS, MERCH, AND SOCIAL

Outside the site, the identity shows up on Discord, X, Twitch, merch, and the arcade. After Darc, the club’s Twitch show, has its own graphics and a starting-soon animation.

07 / 11
THE WEBSITE

PARC had outgrown its Squarespace site. The club now had four collections, a token, a Twitch show, an arcade, and merch. I designed a new site to bring them together and built it with Claude Code, directing the work and reviewing every screen.

I built the site around the logo’s pixel grid and the club’s island setting. The Clubhouse, Gallery, and PARCade each have their own place in that world. The home page opens with the wordmark on a notched paper card. Inner pages use a jungle canopy, drifting clouds, and a wooden sign for the title and introduction.

The notch shows up everywhere: 6px on buttons, 10px on cards, 12px on panels. Buttons sit on a darker base, lift on hover, and drop when you press them. The motion is pixel-based too. Buttons move in steps, water shifts one cell at a time, and dropdowns open line by line. With reduced motion on, the animated backgrounds hold still.

08 / 11
STATS FIRST

I put Stats first in the navigation so holders could find it fast. It has floor prices, trading volume, holders, and listings for each collection, plus $OAR token data. The numbers come from the ledger and marketplace APIs, and daily snapshots feed the charts, going back to launch.

09 / 11
GALLERY & CLUBHOUSE

In the Gallery, apes hang on clotheslines between two trees. Selecting a frame opens a plaque with the ape’s name. My first version turned wheel input into sideways scrolling. It was awkward to use, so I switched to normal vertical scrolling.

The Clubhouse took three layouts to get right. It ended up with a TV playing the Twitch stream, a trophy shelf, and a corkboard for events, suspended from branches. I checked the ropes at different screen widths to keep them attached.

10 / 11
PARCADE

PARCade is an arcade cabinet with a green CRT, scanlines, a joystick, and buttons that work the menu. On the homepage, a smaller screen shows the game cover next to live high scores, with scenery built from the game’s sprites around it.

I also made Rowboat Racer, where an ape rows down a five-lane river dodging logs, reefs, and ziggurats. I drew the sprites on a 3px grid. The riverbanks change between beach, jungle, rock, and village scenery on each run. The server replays a run before accepting its score on the leaderboard.

11 / 11
MERCH & COMMUNITY

I originally planned to link out to the merch store. Using its API meant I could put the catalog on the site and send people to the store only for checkout. Each section got a small detail of its own. After Darc has TV static, chat bubbles drift past the Discord section, and the LARC teaser has a working terminal. The 404 sign says you rowed off the map.

On a phone

OUTCOME
01
A logo library in print and web formats: the wide logo, the square lockup, and the oar
02
PARC Pixel: three weights plus a mono, 56 glyphs each, the only typeface on the site
03
parcxrpl.com: seven pages plus the error pages, live since September 2026
04
Live data from the ledger, xrp.cafe, the AMM, the Fourthwall storefront, and the game leaderboard

JADE AESTHETICS ->

text:
XRP.CAFE
XRP.CAFE

I cofounded xrp.cafe, an NFT marketplace on the XRP Ledger, and was its founding designer. I made the identity, and from 2021 to 2024 I made its campaign graphics, animations, event booths, and community content too.

ROLE
Founding designer
TOOLS
Illustrator, After Effects
LIVE
xrp.cafe
->
01 / 04
THE COFFEE MUG

We wanted xrp.cafe to feel like a friendly place to spend time. A smiling coffee mug suited the name and gave us a character to use in social posts and community chats.

I started with the logo, then drew versions of the mug with different outfits and accessories for campaigns and community events.

The same mug became a Halloween pumpkin, went to a beach BBQ, and turned Super Saiyan. I could make something for each occasion while keeping the character recognizable.

02 / 04
MOTION GRAPHICS

“Explore, Create, Trade” is a short vertical animation I made for social feeds, with big type, moving characters, and the brand’s blue background. It had to read on a phone while someone scrolled past.

Other animations covered product launches, feature announcements, and event recaps.

03 / 04
SOCIAL & EVENTS

Most of it went out on Twitter/X, Instagram, and Discord. With several posts a week, I kept making new graphics and writing copy for launches, partnerships, seasonal posts, and community milestones.

I also designed booths, backdrops, banners, and merch for Consensus, Permissionless, and ETH Denver, using the same mug characters people knew from our posts.

Campaigns

Events

04 / 04
OUTCOME

The work included more than ten social campaigns, motion graphics, and event booths, plus campaign graphics for a VeSea charity event that raised $33K for St. Jude. By mid-2026, the marketplace had 32K followers, $16.2M in volume, and 6.7M transactions.

title: First Ledger: brand for a trading platform / Timothy Ali
text:
FIRST LEDGER
FIRST LEDGER

I spent about a year on the identity for First Ledger, a token trading platform from the team behind xrp.cafe. I designed the logo, the type, and the brand guidelines, plus layouts for putting it next to xrp.cafe and partner logos.

ROLE
Brand designer
TIMELINE
About a year
TOOLS
Illustrator
LIVE
firstledger.net
->
01 / 05
PENCIL + PAPER = LEDGER

First Ledger gives people access to the XRP Ledger’s decentralized exchange through a Telegram bot and a web app. The mark is a diagonal pencil on a rounded square of paper. Pencil and paper make a ledger, a place to record transactions.

It had to read in a Telegram chat, a browser tab, and a small mobile header. I kept the shape simple enough to recognize at those sizes, then used it across the rest of the identity.

02 / 05
LOCKUPS & TYPOGRAPHY

The primary lockup pairs the icon with “FIRST LEDGER” in heavy, extended type. A shorter “FL” version fits smaller spaces. Both have clear-space rules measured from the icon.

Everything is set in Helvetica Neue Extended, with Heavy for headlines, Medium for subheads, and Roman for body copy.

03 / 05
BRAND PILLARS

Fun: “a lil meme never hurt anyone.” Reliable: “passion and years of experience.” Fast: “we’re first for a reason.”

The brand had to work for jokes and memes as well as product announcements and partnership decks. Those three traits kept the tone the same across both.

04 / 05
CO-BRANDING GUIDELINES

First Ledger and xrp.cafe often appear together. I documented the logo sizes and spacing for those layouts so the team could reuse them.

The guidelines cover partner logos too, so the team has something to check when they put together listings, reports, and joint campaigns.

05 / 05
OUTCOME

I handed over the logo, the lockups, the type system, and the guidelines, co-branding layouts included. By mid-2026, First Ledger had passed $1.2B in transaction volume, 165K peak users, and more than 2M wallets created.

NEXT / [05]
XRP.CAFE ->
[04] / 007

title: Do Androids Dream? A title sequence / Timothy Ali

controls.text: Play video: Do Androids Dream title sequence, about forty seconds, black on yellow, silent here

text:
DO ANDROIDS DREAM?
DO ANDROIDS DREAM?

For a class project at RMCAD, I made a title sequence for an imagined adaptation of Philip K. Dick’s Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, the novel behind Blade Runner. I designed and animated it in yellow and black, using flat shapes and Saul Bass’s title work as a reference. The film credits are fictional.

ROLE
Designer and animator
TIMELINE
Class project at RMCAD, 2023
TOOLS
After Effects, Illustrator

Watch it with sound on YouTube
->

01 / 03
THE CONCEPT

I started by reducing the city to silhouettes. Towers, roads, a sun, and a lone figure were enough to build the sequence on.

Against the yellow sky, the black buildings feel heavy. I used changes in scale and composition to give the sequence variety within those two colors.

02 / 03
VISUAL LANGUAGE

I drew the skyline in Illustrator as flat vector shapes, then animated it in After Effects. The buildings dwarf the figure, which gives the city its scale without much detail.

A little chromatic aberration fringes the edges with color, like electronic interference, so the clean shapes feel slightly unstable.

03 / 03
MOTION & PACING

The 40-second sequence moves from the title into the skyline, then breaks the perspective with an inverted city and road. The final shots bring in the sun and a figure surrounded by radiating architecture.

Changes in perspective connect the scenes and make the city feel disorienting. I cut the sequence to The Doors’ “End of the Night.” The video here is silent. You can watch it with sound on YouTube.

title: Jade Aesthetics: medical spa websites / Timothy Ali
text:
JADE AESTHETICS
JADE AESTHETICS

I designed and built two websites for Jade Aesthetics, a medical spa in Wheaton, Illinois. The first launched in Framer. When the practice needed individual treatment pages, I rebuilt it in Next.js, keeping the visual style I’d developed for the first site.

ROLE
Designer & developer
TIMELINE
Ongoing · project-based freelance
TOOLS
Framer (V1), Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Vercel, Claude Code (V2)
LIVE
jadeaesthetics.co
->
01 / 05
VERSION ONE: THE LAUNCH SITE

The practice came to me with a logo, and I built the look of the site around it: jade green and warm gold on cream backgrounds, with photos of the treatment rooms so visitors could get a feel for the place.

The Framer site introduced the practice, its services, and its approach to care. It gave the team a website while the business was getting off the ground.

02 / 05
WHY I REBUILT IT

The practice needed individual treatment pages that people could find through search. I built a shared template in Next.js so each page could have its own content, metadata, and structured data.

The template also made it easier to add treatments. Each gets its own URL and follows the same structure, so the team doesn’t need a new page design for every service.

03 / 05
VERSION TWO: TREATMENT PAGES

I used Next.js and Tailwind CSS for the rebuild. I designed the page structure and components, then worked with Claude Code to build them and reviewed the results. The site uses server-rendered pages, individual metadata, structured data, breadcrumbs, and a generated sitemap.

The rebuild has more than 30 pages: service categories, 16 treatment pages, two skincare lines, team bios, FAQs, financing, and contact details. Each treatment page explains what the procedure is, who it’s for, what to expect, and how recovery goes, so people can read all of that before they book.

04 / 05
KEEPING THE VISUAL IDENTITY

The rebuild kept the first site’s look, with Space Grotesk for headings and Sora for text. I turned the service cards, FAQ accordions, testimonial carousels, and contact blocks into reusable components, which kept the pages consistent as there got to be more of them.

05 / 05
OUTCOME

The rebuild went live in about two months with more than 30 pages, 16 of them treatment pages. The old URLs redirect to the new ones, and the site still looks like the Framer version.

NEXT / [04]
FIRST LEDGER ->

I designed and built two websites for Jade Aesthetics, a medical spa in Wheaton, Illinois. The first launched in Framer. When the practice needed individual treatment pages, I rebuilt it in Next.js, keeping the visual style I’d developed for the first site.

ROLE
Designer & developer
TIMELINE
Ongoing · project-based freelance
TOOLS
Framer (V1), Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Vercel, Claude Code (V2)
LIVE
jadeaesthetics.co
->
01 / 05
VERSION ONE: THE LAUNCH SITE

The practice came to me with a logo, and I built the look of the site around it: jade green and warm gold on cream backgrounds, with photos of the treatment rooms so visitors could get a feel for the place.

The Framer site introduced the practice, its services, and its approach to care. It gave the team a website while the business was getting off the ground.

02 / 05
WHY I REBUILT IT

The practice needed individual treatment pages that people could find through search. I built a shared template in Next.js so each page could have its own content, metadata, and structured data.

The template also made it easier to add treatments. Each gets its own URL and follows the same structure, so the team doesn’t need a new page design for every service.

03 / 05
VERSION TWO: TREATMENT PAGES

I used Next.js and Tailwind CSS for the rebuild. I designed the page structure and components, then worked with Claude Code to build them and reviewed the results. The site uses server-rendered pages, individual metadata, structured data, breadcrumbs, and a generated sitemap.

The rebuild has more than 30 pages: service categories, 16 treatment pages, two skincare lines, team bios, FAQs, financing, and contact details. Each treatment page explains what the procedure is, who it’s for, what to expect, and how recovery goes, so people can read all of that before they book.

04 / 05
KEEPING THE VISUAL IDENTITY

The rebuild kept the first site’s look, with Space Grotesk for headings and Sora for text. I turned the service cards, FAQ accordions, testimonial carousels, and contact blocks into reusable components, which kept the pages consistent as there got to be more of them.

05 / 05
OUTCOME

The rebuild went live in about two months with more than 30 pages, 16 of them treatment pages. The old URLs redirect to the new ones, and the site still looks like the Framer version.

title: FirstStrike Research: brand identity / Timothy Ali
text:
FIRSTSTRIKE RESEARCH
FIRSTSTRIKE RESEARCH

FirstStrike Research is a veteran-owned financial research blog about American markets. I designed its logo, colors, type, and brand guidelines.

ROLE
Sole brand designer
TOOLS
Illustrator, Figma
01 / 05
THE BRIEF

The client brought a rough mood board of retro print references and wanted the brand to feel direct and credible. From there I worked out a heavy wordmark, halftone details, and a blue palette.

02 / 05
LOGO & WORDMARK

The wordmark uses heavy italic type with a halftone pattern trailing off the F. The forward lean suits the name, and the dots bring in the newsprint reference from the brief.

I made horizontal and stacked lockups, plus an icon for favicons and avatars. Each has versions for light and dark backgrounds.

03 / 05
COLOR & TYPE

Electric Blue (#003DFF) is the main color, with Midnight Black and Ice White. Soft Mint, Signal Coral, and Amber Pulse widen the palette for charts and graphics. Headlines are in Helvetica Heavy and body copy in Helvetica Medium.

04 / 05
PRINT TEXTURE

I added grain to a blue-to-cyan gradient for a printed texture, then used it across social cards, editorial layouts, and billboard mockups.

05 / 05
OUTCOME

I handed over the logo files and guidelines for color, typography, and backgrounds, with examples on business cards, social graphics, and billboards.

title: Toolbox: desktop app for brand files / Timothy Ali
text:
TOOLBOX
TOOLBOX

I designed and built Toolbox for the file prep that comes with brand work. It packages logos for print and web, exports color palettes, makes type specimens, and converts images. It runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux, and every tool also works from the command line or through an AI assistant over MCP.

ROLE
Designer & developer
TIMELINE
Started August 2026; rebuilt in Rust for version 1.2.0, October 2026
TOOLS
Rust, Tauri, Leptos, Claude Code
LIVE
Downloads and guides
->
01 / 03
FOUR TOOLS

Lockup turns logo SVGs into a folder of print and web files. You get color, black, and white versions in several sizes, a README, and social images if you want them. PDF and EPS exports can carry named Pantone spot colors. Palette turns a set of colors into code, swatches, and reference sheets. Specimen makes type sheets from your installed fonts, and Convert changes image formats, sizes, and compression.

Projects keep each client or job together. You can save the settings, reopen the work later, and export it again. Every export goes in a new folder, so earlier deliveries are left alone. The library and the exported files stay on your computer.

Palette extracts colors from artwork. Specimen previews a type sheet.

Convert shows the output size for each format. The app opens on your projects.

02 / 03
APP, COMMAND LINE, AND AGENTS

The command line and the MCP server take the same settings as the app, so a script or an AI assistant can inspect source files, preview results, reopen saved work, and export without opening a window.

An assistant can also sort a client folder. It plans the moves, and Toolbox checks them, shows a dry run first, and keeps an undo record. Nothing gets deleted.

The app shares its terminal look and several components with this site.

03 / 03
OUTCOME

Version 1.2.0 is the first one built in Rust, with Tauri and Leptos instead of Electron and Svelte. I kept the old app as the reference and only deleted it once the new one matched it.

I also took out the chat window and the AI built into the app. I drive Toolbox from my own model over MCP now, so organizing folders became MCP and command-line tools. The app opens on your projects, and every tool has a smooth or hard edges setting.

Toolbox is available for macOS, Windows, and Linux. The macOS builds are signed and notarized, and Linux builds come as AppImage and deb packages. I dropped Windows at 1.1.0 because of the cost of code signing. It’s back in 1.2.0, unsigned. Downloads and guides are on this site.

title: Lockup / Toolbox / Timothy Ali
text:
LOCKUP
LOCKUP

Turn your logo variations into a set of print and web files.

IN
Vector SVGs
OUT
PNG, JPEG, SVG, PDF, EPS, README
GET IT
Download for macOS, Windows, or Linux
->
WHEN TO USE IT

Lockup is for preparing a set of logo files for a client, developer, or printer. Add an SVG for each logo variation, then pick the formats, colors, and sizes you need. You can assign CMYK and Pantone print colors in the app, the CLI, or MCP. For one-off image conversions, use Convert.

EXPORTED FILES

You get WEB and PRINT folders, sorted by logo variation, color treatment, and size, plus a README that explains what’s in them. Web files come as PNG, JPEG, and SVG, and print files as JPEG, PDF, and EPS.

CLI & MCP

Set up the toolbox command using the linked guide, then run this example with your own inputs. The options below work with both the CLI and MCP.

toolbox lockup logo.svg --print none --padding 0.1 --out .
--action <export|inspect|preview|library-list|library-get|library-remove>
Export files, inspect settings and the output plan without writing, render previews, or manage saved work. Convert previews write the selected output formats; other tools write PNG. Specimen also lists fonts. Default: export.
--saved <value>
Saved-work ID to reopen. Explicit options override its settings. Required for library-get and library-remove.
--save
Save the completed export to the app library, or update the reopened record. Defaults to false for scripts. Default: false.
--name <value>
Package name used in the folder and file names.
--variations <json>
Per-input overrides as JSON: [{"index":0,"name":"Horizontal","padding":0.1,"social":true,"socialPadding":0.12}]. Index is zero-based in input order.
--palette <json>
Color overrides as JSON: [{"sourceHex":"#D32F05","hex":"#FF4400","cmyk":[0,73,100,0],"pantone":"172 C"}]. Inspect first to find sourceHex values. CMYK is in percent.
--padVectors
Apply variation padding to SVG, PDF, and EPS as well as raster files. Default: false.
--socialPadding <number>
Padding for square social versions; per-variation settings override this value. Default: 0.12.
--previewDark
Use a dark plate in PNG previews and library thumbnails. Default: false.
--input <values…>
Paths of the logo SVGs, one per variation (horizontal, stacked, mark). You can supply these values without --input. Required unless you’re reopening saved work or querying the library.
--web <jpeg|png|svg>
Web file types to include. Pass an empty array to skip web output. Default: jpeg, png, svg.
--print <eps|jpeg|pdf>
Print file types to include. Pass an empty array to skip print output. Default: eps, jpeg, pdf.
--treatments <color|black|white>
Colourways to build. Default: color, black, white.
--sizes <large|medium|small>
Raster sizes: large is 3000px, medium 1500px, small 600px on the long edge. Default: large, medium, small.
--padding <number>
Clear space around the mark, as a fraction of the long edge (0 to 0.25). Default: 0.
--social
Also emit a square profile-picture version of each variation (web only). Default: false.
--edgeSmoothing <smooth|hard>
Edges in the PNG and JPEG files: 'smooth' anti-aliases them; 'hard' turns anti-aliasing off, so every pixel is fully in or out. SVG, PDF and EPS are unchanged. Default: smooth.
--out <value>
Folder to write into. A fresh subfolder is created inside it, so nothing is overwritten. Required for export and preview.

CLI & MCP

Set up the toolbox command using the linked guide, then run this example with your own inputs. The options below work with both the CLI and MCP.

toolbox palette '#D32F05' '#003A5D' --name Acme --out .
--action <export|inspect|preview|library-list|library-get|library-remove>
Export files, inspect settings and the output plan without writing, render previews, or manage saved work. Convert previews write the selected output formats; other tools write PNG. Specimen also lists fonts. Default: export.
--saved <value>
Saved-work ID to reopen. Explicit options override its settings. Required for library-get and library-remove.
--save
Save the completed export to the app library, or update the reopened record. Defaults to false for scripts. Default: false.
--entries <json>
Ordered swatches as JSON: [{"name":"Orange","hex":"#D32F05","cmyk":[0,78,98,17],"pantone":"1665 C"}]. Replaces extracted or saved entries; colors and samples then append.
--samples <json>
Sample image colors at normalized coordinates: [{"image":0,"x":0.5,"y":0.5}]. Image indices come from inspect.
--extract
Add dominant image colors automatically. Disable to select only explicit samples or entries. Default: true.
--colors <values…>
Hex colours to include, for example ['#D32F05', '#003A5D']. You can supply these values without --colors.
--input <values…>
Paths of artwork to pull colours from. SVGs contribute their exact fills; images contribute their dominant colours. Combines with `colors`.
--name <value>
Palette name, used for the file names and the sheet heading. Default: Palette.
--outputs <css|tokens|ase|sheet>
Which files to write. Default: css, tokens, ase, sheet.
--edgeSmoothing <smooth|hard>
Edges on the swatch sheet (PNG, and the image inside its PDF): 'smooth' anti-aliases them; 'hard' turns anti-aliasing off. Default: smooth.
--out <value>
Folder to write into. A fresh subfolder is created inside it, so nothing is overwritten. Required for export and preview.

title: Convert / Toolbox / Timothy Ali
text:
CONVERT
CONVERT

Change image formats, resize images, and adjust compression.

IN
PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP, ICO, AVIF, SVG; HEIC, TIFF, PSD on macOS
OUT
PNG, JPEG, WebP, TIFF, PDF
GET IT
Download for macOS, Windows, or Linux
->
WHEN TO USE IT

Convert changes image formats, resizes files, and adjusts compression. On both platforms it reads PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP, ICO, AVIF, and SVG. HEIC, TIFF, and PSD need macOS. For a full package of logo variations, use Lockup.

EXPORTED FILES

title: CLI & MCP / Toolbox / Timothy Ali
text:
CLI & MCP
CLI & MCP

Use Toolbox from a terminal or an AI assistant.

Toolbox includes a command-line interface (CLI) and an MCP server. Use the CLI in your terminal or scripts. MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets an AI assistant find and run the tools. Both work without opening an app window.

SET UP
COMMAND LINE
ADVANCED
OPTIONS
LIST
RUN
SERVE
ORGANIZE
MACOS
/Applications/Toolbox.app/Contents/MacOS/Toolbox
LINUX
toolbox
SET UP THE COMMAND

Install Toolbox first. You can run it from the full executable path shown above, or set up the toolbox shortcut these examples use. On macOS, the command here creates that shortcut. Run the executable directly. The macOS open command won’t send results back to your terminal.

sudo ln -s "/Applications/Toolbox.app/Contents/MacOS/Toolbox" /usr/local/bin/toolbox
THE COMMAND LINE

Choose a tool, add your inputs and options, and set an output folder. Running toolbox without arguments opens the app. The CLI and MCP support all four tools and the same export settings.

toolbox help
# show tools and usage
toolbox convert --help
# show Convert options
toolbox --version
# show the version
toolbox lockup logo.svg --print none --padding 0.1 --out .
toolbox palette '#D32F05' '#003A5D' --name Acme --out .
toolbox specimen --template classic --family Helvetica --out .
toolbox convert a.heic b.png --formats webp --compression 40 --out ~/Desktop
INPUTS
Pass file paths to convert and lockup, or hex colors to palette, without a flag. Relative paths start from your current folder. Put quotes around paths with spaces.
LISTS AND SWITCHES
Separate values with spaces or commas: --formats webp png or --formats=webp,png. Use none to skip a group (--print none) and --no- to turn a switch off (--no-social).
OUTPUT
--out writes into a new folder inside the destination, leaving existing files alone. Add --json for a JSON result. Exit codes: 0 success, 1 failed, 2 invalid; errors go to stderr.
ADVANCED

From version 1.1.0 you can also assign print colors, adjust logo variations, and set font roles. Structured flags like --palette and --roles take a JSON array in quotes. Over MCP, pass the same arrays without quotes. Use inspect to find the colors in your artwork and fonts to list installed families.

--action inspect shows what will be exported without writing files. --action preview with --out saves previews. Add --save to keep the settings in the app’s library, then reopen them with the savedID in the result.

Version 1.2.0 adds --edgeSmoothing to every tool. hard turns off anti-aliasing in the raster files, so every pixel is fully in or out. Vector files don’t change. smooth is the default.

toolbox lockup logo.svg --action inspect --json
toolbox lockup logo.svg --name Acme --out ./exports --palette '[{"sourceHex":"#D32F05","cmyk":[0,78,98,17],"pantone":"1665 C"}]'
toolbox specimen --action fonts --json
toolbox specimen --title "Acme type" --out ./exports --roles '[{"label":"Heading","family":"Helvetica","face":"Bold","size":40}]'
toolbox lockup logo.svg --edgeSmoothing hard --out ./exports
toolbox lockup logo.svg --print none --save --out ./exports --json
toolbox lockup --action library-list --json
toolbox lockup --saved RECORD_ID --action inspect --json
toolbox lockup --saved RECORD_ID --padding 0.15 --save --out ./exports --json
OPTIONS

Each tool’s page lists its flags and defaults. To check your installed version, run toolbox <tool> --help, or toolbox list for the option schemas as JSON.

LOCKUP OPTIONS
->
PALETTE OPTIONS
->
SPECIMEN OPTIONS
->
CONVERT OPTIONS
->
LIST

Run toolbox list to get a JSON catalog of all four tools and the organize steps, with descriptions, argument schemas, and examples. For one tool, run toolbox describe and the tool’s name.

toolbox list
# every tool, as JSON
toolbox describe convert
# one tool, as JSON
RUN

Pass the tool name and arguments to --run as a JSON object. Toolbox returns the output folder, file names, and any warnings. A failed job returns "ok": false with an error message and exits with code 1. Replace the example paths with your own.

toolbox --run '{"tool":"convert","args":{
  "input":["/Users/me/Pictures/IMG_0001.heic"],
  "formats":["webp"],
  "compression":40,
  "longestEdge":2000,
  "out":"/Users/me/Desktop"
}}'
{
  "ok": true,
  "tool": "convert",
  "outputDir": "/Users/me/Desktop/Converted",
  "files": ["IMG_0001.webp"],
  "warnings": []
}
SERVE

To connect an AI assistant, add this server configuration to its MCP settings, using the executable path for your platform. --mcp serves the tools over standard input and output. Claude Code reads project settings from .mcp.json.

Then ask your assistant to convert screenshots to WebP, package logo SVGs, pull colors from artwork, or tidy a client folder. Tell it where the source files are and which folder to save to.

toolbox --mcp
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "toolbox": {
      "command": "/Applications/Toolbox.app/Contents/MacOS/Toolbox",
      "args": ["--mcp"]
    }
  }
}
ORGANIZE A FOLDER

Toolbox can sort a client folder, but it doesn’t decide where things go. Your assistant plans the moves. Toolbox lists the folder, checks the plan, moves the files, and keeps a record so you can undo it. Over MCP the steps are organize_scan, organize_apply, organize_undo, and organize_history. In a terminal they’re toolbox organize scan, apply, undo, and history. Each one prints JSON.

toolbox organize scan ~/Clients/Acme
toolbox organize apply ~/Clients/Acme --dryRun \
  --moves '[{"from":"IMG_0042.jpg","to":"Photos/IMG_0042.jpg"}]' \
  --keep '[{"path":"logo.svg"}]'
toolbox organize apply ~/Clients/Acme \
  --moves '[{"from":"IMG_0042.jpg","to":"Photos/IMG_0042.jpg"}]' \
  --keep '[{"path":"logo.svg"}]'
toolbox organize history ~/Clients/Acme
toolbox organize undo JOURNAL_ID
1. SCAN
Lists what’s in the folder, numbered, with duplicate files grouped. Nothing moves.
2. DRY RUN
Send the planned moves with --dryRun, or dryRun: true over MCP. Toolbox checks them and changes nothing. Show the user the result.
3. APPLY
Only after they agree, send the same plan without --dryRun. Toolbox checks the folder again first and leaves out any unsafe move, with the reason. Duplicate copies go to a .toolbox-recovery folder inside it. Nothing is deleted.
4. UNDO
Every apply returns a journal ID. toolbox organize undo with that ID puts everything back, and history lists past runs. Undo the newest first.

# every tool, as JSON
toolbox describe convert
# one tool, as JSON
RUN

Pass the tool name and arguments to --run as a JSON object. Toolbox returns the output folder, file names, and any warnings. A failed job returns "ok": false with an error message and exits with code 1. Replace the example paths with your own.

toolbox --run '{"tool":"convert","args":{
  "input":["/Users/me/Pictures/IMG_0001.heic"],
  "formats":["webp"],
  "compression":40,
  "longestEdge":2000,
  "out":"/Users/me/Desktop"
}}'
{
  "ok": true,
  "tool": "convert",
  "outputDir": "/Users/me/Desktop/Converted",
  "files": ["IMG_0001.webp"],
  "warnings": []
}
SERVE

To connect an AI assistant, add this server configuration to its MCP settings, using the executable path for your platform. --mcp serves the tools over standard input and output. Claude Code reads project settings from .mcp.json.

Then ask your assistant to convert screenshots to WebP, package logo SVGs, pull colors from artwork, or tidy a client folder. Tell it where the source files are and which folder to save to.

toolbox --mcp
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "toolbox": {
      "command": "/Applications/Toolbox.app/Contents/MacOS/Toolbox",
      "args": ["--mcp"]
    }
  }
}
ORGANIZE A FOLDER

Toolbox can sort a client folder, but it doesn’t decide where things go. Your assistant plans the moves. Toolbox lists the folder, checks the plan, moves the files, and keeps a record so you can undo it. Over MCP the steps are organize_scan, organize_apply, organize_undo, and organize_history. In a terminal they’re toolbox organize scan, apply, undo, and history. Each one prints JSON.

toolbox organize scan ~/Clients/Acme
toolbox organize apply ~/Clients/Acme --dryRun \
  --moves '[{"from":"IMG_0042.jpg","to":"Photos/IMG_0042.jpg"}]' \
  --keep '[{"path":"logo.svg"}]'
toolbox organize apply ~/Clients/Acme \
  --moves '[{"from":"IMG_0042.jpg","to":"Photos/IMG_0042.jpg"}]' \
  --keep '[{"path":"logo.svg"}]'
toolbox organize history ~/Clients/Acme
toolbox organize undo JOURNAL_ID
1. SCAN
Lists what’s in the folder, numbered, with duplicate files grouped. Nothing moves.
2. DRY RUN
Send the planned moves with --dryRun, or dryRun: true over MCP. Toolbox checks them and changes nothing. Show the user the result.
3. APPLY
Only after they agree, send the same plan without --dryRun. Toolbox checks the folder again first and leaves out any unsafe move, with the reason. Duplicate copies go to a .toolbox-recovery folder inside it. Nothing is deleted.
4. UNDO
Every apply returns a journal ID. toolbox organize undo with that ID puts everything back, and history lists past runs. Undo the newest first.
ALL FOUR TOOLS ->

title: PARC: NFT club identity and website / Timothy Ali

controls.text: Play video: PARC After Darc starting-soon screen: a pixel sun over the sea with a rowboat drifting p

text:
PARC
PARC

I cofounded Pixel Ape Rowboat Club in 2021 and have led its branding and art direction since. In 2026, I redesigned the identity around the apes’ 5×5 grid and made a typeface for it, PARC Pixel. Then I built a new website with live stats, a gallery, merch, and a rowing game.

ROLE
Cofounder · brand, art direction & website
TEAM
Cofounders xrpl_adam, sloppy, and stove
TIMELINE
Ongoing · site live since September 2026
TOOLS
Illustrator, Python (fontTools), SvelteKit, Svelte 5, TypeScript, Canvas, Vercel, Neon, Claude Code
LIVE
parcxrpl.com
->
01 / 11
WHERE IT STARTED

PARC started in November 2021 as a joke. People were treating pixel apes as status symbols, and we thought that was ridiculous. Bored Apes had yachts. Ours had rowboats. 10,000 pixel apes on the XRP Ledger, no clout included.

People stayed anyway. By 2026, PARC had four collections, a Twitch show, an arcade, merch, and its own lore. I run it with xrpl_adam on development, sloppy on marketing, and stove drawing the apes with me. The old identity no longer matched what we were making.

The apes were drawn with the Game Boy Advance Pokémon games in mind: flat color, chunky pixels, sprites you could recognize at a glance. We built them a world of islands, rowboats, volcanoes, and wooden huts, and the rebrand had to look like it belonged there.

02 / 11
AN EARLIER DIRECTION

Around 2024, I tried splitting the club into three branches: The Rowboat Club with an oar, The Parcade with a red joystick, and The Nightclub with a red microphone, each with a black pixel wordmark. We liked how it looked, but it felt too serious and dark for PARC, so we set it aside.

Set aside, around 2024

03 / 11
REDRAWING THE LOGO

The old logo was a cartoon ape with thick outlines and a bubbly wordmark. It didn’t look much like the pixel art around it. I drew the new logo on the apes’ 5×5 grid and put it on a white sign with notched corners.

The team was attached to the old identity and worried about how the community would react. This time I showed them the finished logo on its sign and asked them to trust me. The comments after launch were encouraging.

Before, 2021 / after, 2026

THE REACTION
01
“I know I like the new banner and logo” / RedHotDankMoist, Discord
02
“Love it, great website update, looks amazing” / @BrandoWoodz, X
04 / 11
LOGO, COLOR, AND SPACING

I made a wide logo, a square lockup, and an oar badge, all on the same cell grid with notched corners and two cells of clear space around them. The final artwork is merged paths, so it goes straight into print and web files.

The palette has five colors. The logo uses four of them, and everything else uses one at a time. I gave hex values for web and CMYK for print, and ruled out yellow type on white because it’s hard to read.

The oar works as a favicon, a badge, and a divider. I also put it on the typeface’s equals key so it’s easy to use in a line of text.

05 / 11
THE TYPEFACE

I built PARC Pixel from the four letters in the logo, keeping their one-cell strokes, open counters, and stepped diagonals. Scripts generate the family from the logo’s grid: three weights and a monospaced version for scores and prices, with 56 glyphs in each. It took four days from the first glyph to the finished family.

The scripts struggled with some characters, especially the number 2. I built a small editor to place pixels by hand, then used the scripts to compile the fonts. I drew 29 glyphs across the family this way, including the bold 2, the oar, and all three at-signs, and checked them in words at reading size.

06 / 11
STREAMS, MERCH, AND SOCIAL

Outside the site, the identity shows up on Discord, X, Twitch, merch, and the arcade. After Darc, the club’s Twitch show, has its own graphics and a starting-soon animation.

07 / 11
THE WEBSITE

PARC had outgrown its Squarespace site. The club now had four collections, a token, a Twitch show, an arcade, and merch. I designed a new site to bring them together and built it with Claude Code, directing the work and reviewing every screen.

I built the site around the logo’s pixel grid and the club’s island setting. The Clubhouse, Gallery, and PARCade each have their own place in that world. The home page opens with the wordmark on a notched paper card. Inner pages use a jungle canopy, drifting clouds, and a wooden sign for the title and introduction.

The notch shows up everywhere: 6px on buttons, 10px on cards, 12px on panels. Buttons sit on a darker base, lift on hover, and drop when you press them. The motion is pixel-based too. Buttons move in steps, water shifts one cell at a time, and dropdowns open line by line. With reduced motion on, the animated backgrounds hold still.

08 / 11
STATS FIRST

I put Stats first in the navigation so holders could find it fast. It has floor prices, trading volume, holders, and listings for each collection, plus $OAR token data. The numbers come from the ledger and marketplace APIs, and daily snapshots feed the charts, going back to launch.

09 / 11
GALLERY & CLUBHOUSE

In the Gallery, apes hang on clotheslines between two trees. Selecting a frame opens a plaque with the ape’s name. My first version turned wheel input into sideways scrolling. It was awkward to use, so I switched to normal vertical scrolling.

The Clubhouse took three layouts to get right. It ended up with a TV playing the Twitch stream, a trophy shelf, and a corkboard for events, suspended from branches. I checked the ropes at different screen widths to keep them attached.

10 / 11
PARCADE

PARCade is an arcade cabinet with a green CRT, scanlines, a joystick, and buttons that work the menu. On the homepage, a smaller screen shows the game cover next to live high scores, with scenery built from the game’s sprites around it.

I also made Rowboat Racer, where an ape rows down a five-lane river dodging logs, reefs, and ziggurats. I drew the sprites on a 3px grid. The riverbanks change between beach, jungle, rock, and village scenery on each run. The server replays a run before accepting its score on the leaderboard.

11 / 11
MERCH & COMMUNITY

I originally planned to link out to the merch store. Using its API meant I could put the catalog on the site and send people to the store only for checkout. Each section got a small detail of its own. After Darc has TV static, chat bubbles drift past the Discord section, and the LARC teaser has a working terminal. The 404 sign says you rowed off the map.

On a phone

OUTCOME
01
A logo library in print and web formats: the wide logo, the square lockup, and the oar
02
PARC Pixel: three weights plus a mono, 56 glyphs each, the only typeface on the site
03
parcxrpl.com: seven pages plus the error pages, live since September 2026
04
Live data from the ledger, xrp.cafe, the AMM, the Fourthwall storefront, and the game leaderboard
NEXT / [03]

[02] / 007

controls.text: Play video: PARC After Darc starting-soon screen: a pixel sun over the sea with a rowboat drifting p

text:
PARC
PARC

I cofounded Pixel Ape Rowboat Club in 2021 and have led its branding and art direction since. In 2026, I redesigned the identity around the apes’ 5×5 grid and made a typeface for it, PARC Pixel. Then I built a new website with live stats, a gallery, merch, and a rowing game.

ROLE
Cofounder · brand, art direction & website
TEAM
Cofounders xrpl_adam, sloppy, and stove
TIMELINE
Ongoing · site live since September 2026
TOOLS
Illustrator, Python (fontTools), SvelteKit, Svelte 5, TypeScript, Canvas, Vercel, Neon, Claude Code
LIVE
parcxrpl.com
->
01 / 11
WHERE IT STARTED

PARC started in November 2021 as a joke. People were treating pixel apes as status symbols, and we thought that was ridiculous. Bored Apes had yachts. Ours had rowboats. 10,000 pixel apes on the XRP Ledger, no clout included.

People stayed anyway. By 2026, PARC had four collections, a Twitch show, an arcade, merch, and its own lore. I run it with xrpl_adam on development, sloppy on marketing, and stove drawing the apes with me. The old identity no longer matched what we were making.

The apes were drawn with the Game Boy Advance Pokémon games in mind: flat color, chunky pixels, sprites you could recognize at a glance. We built them a world of islands, rowboats, volcanoes, and wooden huts, and the rebrand had to look like it belonged there.

02 / 11
AN EARLIER DIRECTION

Around 2024, I tried splitting the club into three branches: The Rowboat Club with an oar, The Parcade with a red joystick, and The Nightclub with a red microphone, each with a black pixel wordmark. We liked how it looked, but it felt too serious and dark for PARC, so we set it aside.

SET ASIDE, AROUND 2024

03 / 11
REDRAWING THE LOGO

The old logo was a cartoon ape with thick outlines and a bubbly wordmark. It didn’t look much like the pixel art around it. I drew the new logo on the apes’ 5×5 grid and put it on a white sign with notched corners.

The team was attached to the old identity and worried about how the community would react. This time I showed them the finished logo on its sign and asked them to trust me. The comments after launch were encouraging.

BEFORE, 2021 / AFTER, 2026

THE REACTION
01
“I know I like the new banner and logo” / RedHotDankMoist, Discord
02
“Love it, great website update, looks amazing” / @BrandoWoodz, X
04 / 11
LOGO, COLOR, AND SPACING

I made a wide logo, a square lockup, and an oar badge, all on the same cell grid with notched corners and two cells of clear space around them. The final artwork is merged paths, so it goes straight into print and web files.

The palette has five colors. The logo uses four of them, and everything else uses one at a time. I gave hex values for web and CMYK for print, and ruled out yellow type on white because it’s hard to read.

The oar works as a favicon, a badge, and a divider. I also put it on the typeface’s equals key so it’s easy to use in a line of text.

05 / 11
THE TYPEFACE

I built PARC Pixel from the four letters in the logo, keeping their one-cell strokes, open counters, and stepped diagonals. Scripts generate the family from the logo’s grid: three weights and a monospaced version for scores and prices, with 56 glyphs in each. It took four days from the first glyph to the finished family.

The scripts struggled with some characters, especially the number 2. I built a small editor to place pixels by hand, then used the scripts to compile the fonts. I drew 29 glyphs across the family this way, including the bold 2, the oar, and all three at-signs, and checked them in words at reading size.

06 / 11
STREAMS, MERCH, AND SOCIAL

Outside the site, the identity shows up on Discord, X, Twitch, merch, and the arcade. After Darc, the club’s Twitch show, has its own graphics and a starting-soon animation.

07 / 11
THE WEBSITE

PARC had outgrown its Squarespace site. The club now had four collections, a token, a Twitch show, an arcade, and merch. I designed a new site to bring them together and built it with Claude Code, directing the work and reviewing every screen.

I built the site around the logo’s pixel grid and the club’s island setting. The Clubhouse, Gallery, and PARCade each have their own place in that world. The home page opens with the wordmark on a notched paper card. Inner pages use a jungle canopy, drifting clouds, and a wooden sign for the title and introduction.

The notch shows up everywhere: 6px on buttons, 10px on cards, 12px on panels. Buttons sit on a darker base, lift on hover, and drop when you press them. The motion is pixel-based too. Buttons move in steps, water shifts one cell at a time, and dropdowns open line by line. With reduced motion on, the animated backgrounds hold still.

08 / 11
STATS FIRST

I put Stats first in the navigation so holders could find it fast. It has floor prices, trading volume, holders, and listings for each collection, plus $OAR token data. The numbers come from the ledger and marketplace APIs, and daily snapshots feed the charts, going back to launch.

09 / 11
GALLERY & CLUBHOUSE

In the Gallery, apes hang on clotheslines between two trees. Selecting a frame opens a plaque with the ape’s name. My first version turned wheel input into sideways scrolling. It was awkward to use, so I switched to normal vertical scrolling.

The Clubhouse took three layouts to get right. It ended up with a TV playing the Twitch stream, a trophy shelf, and a corkboard for events, suspended from branches. I checked the ropes at different screen widths to keep them attached.

10 / 11
PARCADE

PARCade is an arcade cabinet with a green CRT, scanlines, a joystick, and buttons that work the menu. On the homepage, a smaller screen shows the game cover next to live high scores, with scenery built from the game’s sprites around it.

I also made Rowboat Racer, where an ape rows down a five-lane river dodging logs, reefs, and ziggurats. I drew the sprites on a 3px grid. The riverbanks change between beach, jungle, rock, and village scenery on each run. The server replays a run before accepting its score on the leaderboard.

11 / 11
MERCH & COMMUNITY

I originally planned to link out to the merch store. Using its API meant I could put the catalog on the site and send people to the store only for checkout. Each section got a small detail of its own. After Darc has TV static, chat bubbles drift past the Discord section, and the LARC teaser has a working terminal. The 404 sign says you rowed off the map.

ON A PHONE

OUTCOME
01
A logo library in print and web formats: the wide logo, the square lockup, and the oar
02
PARC Pixel: three weights plus a mono, 56 glyphs each, the only typeface on the site
03
parcxrpl.com: seven pages plus the error pages, live since September 2026
04
Live data from the ledger, xrp.cafe, the AMM, the Fourthwall storefront, and the game leaderboard
NEXT / [03]
JADE AESTHETICS ->
[02] / 007
TELL ME WHAT YOU’RE BUILDING ->

People stayed anyway. By 2026, PARC had four collections, a Twitch show, an arcade, merch, and its own lore. I run it with xrpl_adam on development, sloppy on marketing, and stove drawing the apes with me. The old identity no longer matched what we were making.

The apes were drawn with the Game Boy Advance Pokémon games in mind: flat color, chunky pixels, sprites you could recognize at a glance. We built them a world of islands, rowboats, volcanoes, and wooden huts, and the rebrand had to look like it belonged there.

02 / 11
AN EARLIER DIRECTION

Around 2024, I tried splitting the club into three branches: The Rowboat Club with an oar, The Parcade with a red joystick, and The Nightclub with a red microphone, each with a black pixel wordmark. We liked how it looked, but it felt too serious and dark for PARC, so we set it aside.

Set aside, around 2024

03 / 11
REDRAWING THE LOGO

The old logo was a cartoon ape with thick outlines and a bubbly wordmark. It didn’t look much like the pixel art around it. I drew the new logo on the apes’ 5×5 grid and put it on a white sign with notched corners.

The team was attached to the old identity and worried about how the community would react. This time I showed them the finished logo on its sign and asked them to trust me. The comments after launch were encouraging.

Before, 2021 / after, 2026

THE REACTION
01
“I know I like the new banner and logo” / RedHotDankMoist, Discord
02
“Love it, great website update, looks amazing” / @BrandoWoodz, X
04 / 11
LOGO, COLOR, AND SPACING

I made a wide logo, a square lockup, and an oar badge, all on the same cell grid with notched corners and two cells of clear space around them. The final artwork is merged paths, so it goes straight into print and web files.

The palette has five colors. The logo uses four of them, and everything else uses one at a time. I gave hex values for web and CMYK for print, and ruled out yellow type on white because it’s hard to read.

The oar works as a favicon, a badge, and a divider. I also put it on the typeface’s equals key so it’s easy to use in a line of text.

05 / 11
THE TYPEFACE

I built PARC Pixel from the four letters in the logo, keeping their one-cell strokes, open counters, and stepped diagonals. Scripts generate the family from the logo’s grid: three weights and a monospaced version for scores and prices, with 56 glyphs in each. It took four days from the first glyph to the finished family.

The scripts struggled with some characters, especially the number 2. I built a small editor to place pixels by hand, then used the scripts to compile the fonts. I drew 29 glyphs across the family this way, including the bold 2, the oar, and all three at-signs, and checked them in words at reading size.

06 / 11
STREAMS, MERCH, AND SOCIAL

Outside the site, the identity shows up on Discord, X, Twitch, merch, and the arcade. After Darc, the club’s Twitch show, has its own graphics and a starting-soon animation.

07 / 11
THE WEBSITE

PARC had outgrown its Squarespace site. The club now had four collections, a token, a Twitch show, an arcade, and merch. I designed a new site to bring them together and built it with Claude Code, directing the work and reviewing every screen.

I built the site around the logo’s pixel grid and the club’s island setting. The Clubhouse, Gallery, and PARCade each have their own place in that world. The home page opens with the wordmark on a notched paper card. Inner pages use a jungle canopy, drifting clouds, and a wooden sign for the title and introduction.

The notch shows up everywhere: 6px on buttons, 10px on cards, 12px on panels. Buttons sit on a darker base, lift on hover, and drop when you press them. The motion is pixel-based too. Buttons move in steps, water shifts one cell at a time, and dropdowns open line by line. With reduced motion on, the animated backgrounds hold still.

08 / 11
STATS FIRST

I put Stats first in the navigation so holders could find it fast. It has floor prices, trading volume, holders, and listings for each collection, plus $OAR token data. The numbers come from the ledger and marketplace APIs, and daily snapshots feed the charts, going back to launch.

09 / 11
GALLERY & CLUBHOUSE

In the Gallery, apes hang on clotheslines between two trees. Selecting a frame opens a plaque with the ape’s name. My first version turned wheel input into sideways scrolling. It was awkward to use, so I switched to normal vertical scrolling.

The Clubhouse took three layouts to get right. It ended up with a TV playing the Twitch stream, a trophy shelf, and a corkboard for events, suspended from branches. I checked the ropes at different screen widths to keep them attached.

10 / 11
PARCADE

PARCade is an arcade cabinet with a green CRT, scanlines, a joystick, and buttons that work the menu. On the homepage, a smaller screen shows the game cover next to live high scores, with scenery built from the game’s sprites around it.

I also made Rowboat Racer, where an ape rows down a five-lane river dodging logs, reefs, and ziggurats. I drew the sprites on a 3px grid. The riverbanks change between beach, jungle, rock, and village scenery on each run. The server replays a run before accepting its score on the leaderboard.

11 / 11
MERCH & COMMUNITY

I originally planned to link out to the merch store. Using its API meant I could put the catalog on the site and send people to the store only for checkout. Each section got a small detail of its own. After Darc has TV static, chat bubbles drift past the Discord section, and the LARC teaser has a working terminal. The 404 sign says you rowed off the map.

On a phone

OUTCOME
01
A logo library in print and web formats: the wide logo, the square lockup, and the oar
02
PARC Pixel: three weights plus a mono, 56 glyphs each, the only typeface on the site
03
parcxrpl.com: seven pages plus the error pages, live since September 2026
04
Live data from the ledger, xrp.cafe, the AMM, the Fourthwall storefront, and the game leaderboard

title: xrp.cafe: NFT marketplace identity and motion / Timothy Ali

controls.text: Play video: xrp.cafe Explore Create Trade motion graphic

text:
XRP.CAFE
XRP.CAFE

I cofounded xrp.cafe, an NFT marketplace on the XRP Ledger, and was its founding designer. I made the identity, and from 2021 to 2024 I made its campaign graphics, animations, event booths, and community content too.

ROLE
Founding designer
TOOLS
Illustrator, After Effects
LIVE
xrp.cafe
->
01 / 04
THE COFFEE MUG

We wanted xrp.cafe to feel like a friendly place to spend time. A smiling coffee mug suited the name and gave us a character to use in social posts and community chats.

I started with the logo, then drew versions of the mug with different outfits and accessories for campaigns and community events.

The same mug became a Halloween pumpkin, went to a beach BBQ, and turned Super Saiyan. I could make something for each occasion while keeping the character recognizable.

02 / 04
MOTION GRAPHICS

“Explore, Create, Trade” is a short vertical animation I made for social feeds, with big type, moving characters, and the brand’s blue background. It had to read on a phone while someone scrolled past.

Other animations covered product launches, feature announcements, and event recaps.

03 / 04
SOCIAL & EVENTS

Most of it went out on Twitter/X, Instagram, and Discord. With several posts a week, I kept making new graphics and writing copy for launches, partnerships, seasonal posts, and community milestones.

I also designed booths, backdrops, banners, and merch for Consensus, Permissionless, and ETH Denver, using the same mug characters people knew from our posts.

Campaigns

Events

04 / 04
OUTCOME

The work included more than ten social campaigns, motion graphics, and event booths, plus campaign graphics for a VeSea charity event that raised $33K for St. Jude. By mid-2026, the marketplace had 32K followers, $16.2M in volume, and 6.7M transactions.

title: First Ledger: brand for a trading platform / Timothy Ali
text:
FIRST LEDGER
FIRST LEDGER

I spent about a year on the identity for First Ledger, a token trading platform from the team behind xrp.cafe. I designed the logo, the type, and the brand guidelines, plus layouts for putting it next to xrp.cafe and partner logos.

ROLE
Brand designer
TIMELINE
About a year
TOOLS
Illustrator
LIVE
firstledger.net
->
01 / 05
PENCIL + PAPER = LEDGER

First Ledger gives people access to the XRP Ledger’s decentralized exchange through a Telegram bot and a web app. The mark is a diagonal pencil on a rounded square of paper. Pencil and paper make a ledger, a place to record transactions.

It had to read in a Telegram chat, a browser tab, and a small mobile header. I kept the shape simple enough to recognize at those sizes, then used it across the rest of the identity.

02 / 05
LOCKUPS & TYPOGRAPHY

The primary lockup pairs the icon with “FIRST LEDGER” in heavy, extended type. A shorter “FL” version fits smaller spaces. Both have clear-space rules measured from the icon.

Everything is set in Helvetica Neue Extended, with Heavy for headlines, Medium for subheads, and Roman for body copy.

03 / 05
BRAND PILLARS

Fun: “a lil meme never hurt anyone.” Reliable: “passion and years of experience.” Fast: “we’re first for a reason.”

The brand had to work for jokes and memes as well as product announcements and partnership decks. Those three traits kept the tone the same across both.

04 / 05
CO-BRANDING GUIDELINES

First Ledger and xrp.cafe often appear together. I documented the logo sizes and spacing for those layouts so the team could reuse them.

The guidelines cover partner logos too, so the team has something to check when they put together listings, reports, and joint campaigns.

05 / 05
OUTCOME

I handed over the logo, the lockups, the type system, and the guidelines, co-branding layouts included. By mid-2026, First Ledger had passed $1.2B in transaction volume, 165K peak users, and more than 2M wallets created.

title: First Ledger: brand for a trading platform / Timothy Ali
text:
FIRST LEDGER
FIRST LEDGER

I spent about a year on the identity for First Ledger, a token trading platform from the team behind xrp.cafe. I designed the logo, the type, and the brand guidelines, plus layouts for putting it next to xrp.cafe and partner logos.

ROLE
Brand designer
TIMELINE
About a year
TOOLS
Illustrator
LIVE
firstledger.net
->
01 / 05
PENCIL + PAPER = LEDGER

First Ledger gives people access to the XRP Ledger’s decentralized exchange through a Telegram bot and a web app. The mark is a diagonal pencil on a rounded square of paper. Pencil and paper make a ledger, a place to record transactions.

It had to read in a Telegram chat, a browser tab, and a small mobile header. I kept the shape simple enough to recognize at those sizes, then used it across the rest of the identity.

02 / 05
LOCKUPS & TYPOGRAPHY

The primary lockup pairs the icon with “FIRST LEDGER” in heavy, extended type. A shorter “FL” version fits smaller spaces. Both have clear-space rules measured from the icon.

Everything is set in Helvetica Neue Extended, with Heavy for headlines, Medium for subheads, and Roman for body copy.

03 / 05
BRAND PILLARS

Fun: “a lil meme never hurt anyone.” Reliable: “passion and years of experience.” Fast: “we’re first for a reason.”

The brand had to work for jokes and memes as well as product announcements and partnership decks. Those three traits kept the tone the same across both.

04 / 05
CO-BRANDING GUIDELINES

First Ledger and xrp.cafe often appear together. I documented the logo sizes and spacing for those layouts so the team could reuse them.

The guidelines cover partner logos too, so the team has something to check when they put together listings, reports, and joint campaigns.

05 / 05
OUTCOME

I handed over the logo, the lockups, the type system, and the guidelines, co-branding layouts included. By mid-2026, First Ledger had passed $1.2B in transaction volume, 165K peak users, and more than 2M wallets created.

title: Do Androids Dream? A title sequence / Timothy Ali

controls.text: Play video: Do Androids Dream title sequence, about forty seconds, black on yellow, silent here

text:
DO ANDROIDS DREAM?
DO ANDROIDS DREAM?

For a class project at RMCAD, I made a title sequence for an imagined adaptation of Philip K. Dick’s Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, the novel behind Blade Runner. I designed and animated it in yellow and black, using flat shapes and Saul Bass’s title work as a reference. The film credits are fictional.

ROLE
Designer and animator
TIMELINE
Class project at RMCAD, 2023
TOOLS
After Effects, Illustrator

Watch it with sound on YouTube
->

01 / 03
THE CONCEPT

I started by reducing the city to silhouettes. Towers, roads, a sun, and a lone figure were enough to build the sequence on.

Against the yellow sky, the black buildings feel heavy. I used changes in scale and composition to give the sequence variety within those two colors.

02 / 03
VISUAL LANGUAGE

I drew the skyline in Illustrator as flat vector shapes, then animated it in After Effects. The buildings dwarf the figure, which gives the city its scale without much detail.

A little chromatic aberration fringes the edges with color, like electronic interference, so the clean shapes feel slightly unstable.

03 / 03
MOTION & PACING

The 40-second sequence moves from the title into the skyline, then breaks the perspective with an inverted city and road. The final shots bring in the sun and a figure surrounded by radiating architecture.

Changes in perspective connect the scenes and make the city feel disorienting. I cut the sequence to The Doors’ “End of the Night.” The video here is silent. You can watch it with sound on YouTube.

NEXT / [01]

title: Jade Aesthetics: medical spa websites / Timothy Ali
text:
JADE AESTHETICS
JADE AESTHETICS

I designed and built two websites for Jade Aesthetics, a medical spa in Wheaton, Illinois. The first launched in Framer. When the practice needed individual treatment pages, I rebuilt it in Next.js, keeping the visual style I’d developed for the first site.

ROLE
Designer & developer
TIMELINE
Ongoing · project-based freelance
TOOLS
Framer (V1), Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Vercel, Claude Code (V2)
LIVE
jadeaesthetics.co
->
01 / 05
VERSION ONE: THE LAUNCH SITE

The practice came to me with a logo, and I built the look of the site around it: jade green and warm gold on cream backgrounds, with photos of the treatment rooms so visitors could get a feel for the place.

The Framer site introduced the practice, its services, and its approach to care. It gave the team a website while the business was getting off the ground.

02 / 05
WHY I REBUILT IT

The practice needed individual treatment pages that people could find through search. I built a shared template in Next.js so each page could have its own content, metadata, and structured data.

The template also made it easier to add treatments. Each gets its own URL and follows the same structure, so the team doesn’t need a new page design for every service.

03 / 05
VERSION TWO: TREATMENT PAGES

I used Next.js and Tailwind CSS for the rebuild. I designed the page structure and components, then worked with Claude Code to build them and reviewed the results. The site uses server-rendered pages, individual metadata, structured data, breadcrumbs, and a generated sitemap.

The rebuild has more than 30 pages: service categories, 16 treatment pages, two skincare lines, team bios, FAQs, financing, and contact details. Each treatment page explains what the procedure is, who it’s for, what to expect, and how recovery goes, so people can read all of that before they book.

04 / 05
KEEPING THE VISUAL IDENTITY

The rebuild kept the first site’s look, with Space Grotesk for headings and Sora for text. I turned the service cards, FAQ accordions, testimonial carousels, and contact blocks into reusable components, which kept the pages consistent as there got to be more of them.

05 / 05
OUTCOME

The rebuild went live in about two months with more than 30 pages, 16 of them treatment pages. The old URLs redirect to the new ones, and the site still looks like the Framer version.

NEXT / [04]
FIRST LEDGER ->
[03] / 007
TELL ME WHAT YOU’RE BUILDING ->
